title: Krishi Katha: The Farming Seasons
theme: Indian Farming Simulation Across Agricultural Seasons
description: You are Kisan Arjun, a young farmer who has inherited 5 acres of land in a village near Nashik, Maharashtra. Armed with traditional knowledge from your grandfather and modern agricultural science from your Krishi Vigyan Kendra training, you must navigate the three Indian farming seasons -- Kharif (monsoon), Rabi (winter), and Zaid (summer). Plant the right crops, manage water wisely, protect your soil, survive unpredictable monsoons, and make your farm both profitable and sustainable. India's 150 million farming families face these decisions every season. Your choices will teach you why farming is not just a profession in India -- it is the backbone of the nation.
learning_objectives: Understand India's three agricultural seasons (Kharif, Rabi, Zaid) and suitable crops for each
Learn about irrigation methods, water management, and the importance of monsoons in Indian agriculture
Explore sustainable farming practices: organic farming, crop rotation, and soil conservation
Understand government agricultural schemes (PM-KISAN, MSP, PMFBY) and their role in farmer welfare
Develop resource management skills and appreciate the challenges faced by Indian farmers

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are Kisan Arjun managing a 5-acre farm near Nashik, Maharashtra
Each round represents a key decision point across the farming year
Choose which crops to plant, how to manage water, and how to handle agricultural challenges
Monitor Crop Health, Water Supply, Money (INR), and Soil Quality throughout the game
Balance short-term profits with long-term soil health and sustainability
Navigate monsoon uncertainties, market fluctuations, and government policies
tips: Soil quality is your long-term asset -- depleting it for short-term profit is a losing strategy
Water management is the difference between a good harvest and a failed crop
Diversify crops to reduce risk -- monoculture is efficient but vulnerable
Government schemes like PM-KISAN and crop insurance exist to help -- use them
Traditional farming wisdom and modern science together are more powerful than either alone

rounds.title: Round 1: Kharif Season -- What to Plant?
rounds.story: June arrives with dark monsoon clouds gathering over the Sahyadri hills. The Kharif (monsoon) season is here, and your 5 acres of land near Nashik are ready for planting. Your grandfather grew onions and bajra. The Krishi Vigyan Kendra advisor recommends soybean as a cash crop. Your neighbour has made a fortune growing grapes for export but warns it requires massive investment. The monsoon forecast from IMD predicts normal rainfall this year. APMC mandi prices for onions have been volatile but soybean MSP is guaranteed. You must decide what to plant on your primary acreage.
rounds.goal: Choose the right Kharif crop considering monsoon forecasts, market prices, investment needs, and soil suitability.

choices.label: Plant Onions -- Nashik's Signature Crop
choices.feedback: Nashik is India's onion capital, producing 30% of the nation's onions. You plant Agrifound Dark Red variety. Onions need well-drained soil and moderate water. The APMC Lasalgaon mandi (Asia's largest onion market) is just 50 km away. Onion prices are famously volatile -- they can crash to Rs 5/kg or spike to Rs 100/kg. The government's price stabilization fund and NAFED procurement try to stabilize prices, but onion farming remains India's most politically sensitive crop. Governments have literally fallen over onion prices!

choices.label: Plant Soybean -- Guaranteed MSP and Growing Demand
choices.feedback: Soybean is called 'yellow gold' in Maharashtra. It requires less water than onions, fixes nitrogen in the soil (improving soil quality!), and has a guaranteed Minimum Support Price (MSP) from the government. India's MSP system, determined by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), ensures farmers get a minimum return. Soybean oil and meal are in growing demand. Leguminous crops like soybean are part of 'crop rotation' -- they restore soil nutrients that other crops deplete. Your grandfather's bajra followed by your soybean is excellent rotation.

choices.label: Mixed Cropping -- Bajra + Tur Dal + Vegetables
choices.feedback: You follow the traditional Indian practice of mixed cropping (intercropping): bajra (millet) as the main crop, tur (pigeon pea) dal between rows, and seasonal vegetables on the borders. This is exactly how Indian farmers farmed for centuries -- multiple crops reduce pest risk, improve soil health, and ensure food security even if one crop fails. The International Year of Millets (2023) highlighted India's traditional millet-based farming systems. Mixed cropping is scientifically validated 'polyculture' -- nature does not grow monocultures, and neither should smart farmers.

rounds.image_prompt: a lush green field near the Sahyadri hills under dark, looming monsoon clouds, freshly turned soil ready for planting, farming tools scattered, a sense of anticipation in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: The Kharif sowing decision is irreversible for 120 days — farmers who plan their inputs before the monsoon arrives save 20-30% on emergency purchases. In Nashik, the onion gamble is legendary: in good years it pays three times more than soybean, but a glut can crash the mandi price below production cost within a single week. Crop selection is the riskiest and most consequential decision of the farming year.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 2: The Monsoon Gamble -- Irrigation Decisions
rounds.story: Two weeks after planting, the monsoon rains arrive -- but they are erratic. Your village received heavy rain for three days, then nothing for two weeks. IMD calls it a 'monsoon break.' Your crops are wilting. You have three irrigation options: your grandfather's old open well (free but limited water), a new borewell (expensive to drill but reliable), or the recently completed government canal from the Jayakwadi Dam on the Godavari River (subsidized water but requires paperwork and a wait). The Kharif crop needs consistent moisture for the next six weeks or yields will drop dramatically.
rounds.goal: Choose an irrigation strategy that balances cost, reliability, and long-term water sustainability.

choices.label: Use the Traditional Open Well + Micro-Irrigation
choices.feedback: You install drip irrigation from your open well -- delivering water directly to roots with 90% efficiency compared to 30% for flood irrigation. India's Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana (PMKSY) provides 55% subsidy for micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler systems). Maharashtra has been a leader in drip irrigation adoption, largely due to Jain Irrigation's technology. Your well has limited water, but drip irrigation makes every drop count. 'Per drop, more crop' is PMKSY's motto -- and it works.

choices.label: Drill a New Borewell for Reliable Groundwater
choices.feedback: The borewell gives you reliable water, but India is facing a groundwater crisis. India extracts more groundwater than any other country -- 250 billion cubic metres annually. In Maharashtra's Deccan trap region, borewells often go dry within 5-10 years. The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) regulates borewell drilling, but enforcement is weak. Your borewell solves the immediate problem but contributes to long-term water table depletion. Sustainable water management requires balancing extraction with recharge -- something India urgently needs to address.

choices.label: Apply for Government Canal Water from Jayakwadi Dam
choices.feedback: You apply through the Water Users Association for canal irrigation. The Jayakwadi Dam on the Godavari, one of Maharashtra's largest, supplies water to Nashik, Aurangabad, and Jalna districts. Government canal water is subsidized but water distribution is often inequitable -- tail-end farmers get less than head-end farmers. India's irrigation infrastructure, built since the 1950s, covers about 50% of cultivated area. The challenge is not just building dams but ensuring fair and efficient water distribution to all farmers. Your patience with paperwork pays off -- the water arrives just in time.

rounds.image_prompt: a dry, sun-scorched village field with wilting crops under a cloudy sky, puddles from recent rains glistening, irrigation options like a cracked old well and a borewell nearby
rounds.coaching_moment: Maharashtra is groundwater-stressed — the Central Ground Water Board reports over-exploitation in 14 of Nashik's 24 talukas. Drilling a borewell provides certainty but contributes to long-term aquifer depletion that your own children will inherit. Micro-irrigation under PM-KUSUM saves up to 50% of water but requires upfront capital; government canal water has no such cost but comes with bureaucratic uncertainty about timing.

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 3: The Pest Attack
rounds.story: Your crops are growing well when disaster strikes: a massive armyworm infestation attacks your field. The Fall Armyworm -- an invasive species originally from the Americas -- has spread across India since 2018, devastating maize and millet crops. Your grandfather never saw this pest; it is a consequence of globalisation and climate change. The local pesticide dealer pushes expensive chemical spray (Rs 2,000/acre). The Krishi Vigyan Kendra suggests Integrated Pest Management (IPM) using biological controls. A neighbour says neem oil spray (traditional method) works fine. Your crop health is dropping daily.
rounds.goal: Choose a pest management strategy that saves your crop while considering cost, health, and environmental impact.

choices.label: Use Chemical Pesticides for Quick Results
choices.feedback: Chemical pesticides kill the armyworm quickly, but they also kill beneficial insects like ladybugs and honeybees that naturally control pests. India is the world's 4th largest pesticide user. Pesticide residues in food and water are a growing health concern -- the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has set maximum residue limits. The Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984), the world's worst industrial disaster at a pesticide factory, remains a stark reminder of chemical risks. Your crop is saved but your soil biome is damaged.

choices.label: Use Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
choices.feedback: IPM combines biological controls (Trichogramma wasps that parasitize armyworm eggs), pheromone traps, and minimal targeted pesticide use. India's National Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM) promotes this approach. IPM reduces pesticide use by 50-70% while maintaining yields. It takes slightly longer than chemical blitzing but is far more sustainable. The concept mirrors ancient Indian agricultural wisdom -- Kautilya's Arthashastra described pest management methods including biological controls over 2,000 years ago. Science and tradition align.

choices.label: Apply Traditional Neem Oil Spray
choices.feedback: Neem (Azadirachta indica) has been used in Indian agriculture for centuries. Azadirachtin, the active compound, disrupts insect feeding and reproduction. It is biodegradable, safe for beneficial insects, and actually improves soil health. India exports neem-based biopesticides worldwide. However, neem oil is slower-acting against a severe armyworm infestation -- your crop health recovers but not as quickly. Traditional knowledge systems in Indian agriculture, documented in texts like Krishi Parashara (1000 CE) and Vrikshayurveda, contain valuable pest management wisdom that modern science is now validating.

choices.label: Release Natural Predators from KVK
choices.feedback: You obtain Trichogramma egg parasitoids and green lacewing larvae from the Krishi Vigyan Kendra's bio-control lab. These natural predators attack armyworm eggs and larvae without any chemical input. India's network of 731 KVKs (one in almost every district) provides exactly this kind of science-based support to farmers. Biological control is a growing field -- ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research) has developed numerous bio-control agents suited for Indian conditions. Your farm becomes a demonstration site for other farmers. The KVK officer is delighted with the results.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant green field of maize under a bright blue sky, with large, menacing armyworms crawling over the plants, farmers looking worried and discussing strategies amidst the chaos
rounds.coaching_moment: Pest management decisions compound over years, not just seasons. Chemical pesticides solve this season's problem while building resistance in next season's pest population — the pink bollworm that devastated Vidarbha cotton had developed Bt resistance after 15 years of monoculture. IPM is slower but builds a farm ecosystem that self-regulates; the Krishi Vigyan Kendra exists precisely to help farmers make this transition with expert support.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 4: Harvest Time -- Marketing Your Produce
rounds.story: October brings harvest time. Your Kharif crop is ready, and the yield is good despite the challenges. Now comes the critical question: where and how to sell. The local APMC mandi offers a transparent auction system but middlemen (arthiyas) take a commission. The new e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) platform lets you check prices across India and sell digitally. A local food processing company offers a contract at a fixed price -- lower than mandi rates but guaranteed. Your storage capacity is limited; the crop must be sold within two weeks or it will spoil.
rounds.goal: Choose the best marketing strategy for your harvest, understanding India's agricultural market system.

choices.label: Sell at the APMC Mandi Through Traditional Auction
choices.feedback: You take your produce to the APMC mandi where licensed traders bid in open auction. The Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) system, established across India, provides regulated marketplaces. However, middlemen commissions, mandi taxes, and transportation costs eat into your earnings. Farmers typically receive only 15-25% of the final retail price. India's 7,000+ APMC mandis handle most agricultural trade, but reforms are needed to give farmers a larger share. Your produce sells at a decent price, but the system takes its cut.

choices.label: Sell Through e-NAM Digital Platform
choices.feedback: You list your produce on e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market), which connects 1,000+ mandis across India. You discover that traders in Madhya Pradesh are offering 15% more than local prices for your soybean. E-NAM eliminates information asymmetry -- the biggest disadvantage farmers face. Launched in 2016, e-NAM is transforming agricultural marketing by enabling pan-India price discovery. Digital literacy is becoming as important as agricultural knowledge for modern Indian farmers. Your higher price comes from accessing a wider market.

choices.label: Sell to Food Processing Company on Contract
choices.feedback: The food processing company buys your entire harvest at a pre-agreed price. It is less than the mandi rate but the certainty is valuable -- no price risk, no transportation headache, no spoilage worry. Contract farming, promoted under the Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance Act, gives farmers guaranteed buyers. Companies like ITC's e-Choupal, PepsiCo's contract potato farming in Punjab, and Amul's dairy model have shown that farmer-corporate partnerships can work when fair. The trade-off is lower price for lower risk.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling local APMC mandi filled with colorful stalls, farmers displaying fresh produce, excited buyers negotiating prices, sunlight streaming down through a clear blue sky
rounds.coaching_moment: MSP is a floor, not a ceiling. Knowing when and where to sell above MSP requires understanding local mandi dynamics, cold chain access, and the difference between distress selling and strategic timing. e-NAM has transformed price discovery for farmers near connected mandis, but requires smartphone literacy and willingness to negotiate digitally. The best marketing decision often isn't about the highest price — it's about the most reliable price at the right time.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 5: Rabi Season -- The Winter Crop Decision
rounds.story: November arrives and the Rabi (winter) season begins. The monsoon is over, and your land needs a new crop. Rabi crops rely on residual soil moisture and irrigation rather than rain. Wheat and chickpea (chana) are traditional Rabi choices. Your soil analysis from the Soil Health Card (a government initiative) shows your soil is low in nitrogen but rich in potassium. The KVK advisor suggests a nitrogen-fixing crop. Your money situation after Kharif harvest will determine how much you can invest. The winter market also offers good prices for vegetables if you can manage the irrigation.
rounds.goal: Plan your Rabi season planting based on soil health data, available water, and market demand.

choices.label: Plant Chickpea (Chana) -- Fixes Nitrogen + Good MSP
choices.feedback: Chickpea is perfect for your nitrogen-depleted soil -- as a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, naturally fertilizing the soil. India is the world's largest producer and consumer of chickpeas (chana). The Soil Health Card scheme, launched in 2015, has given over 23 crore soil health cards to farmers across India, with tailored fertilizer recommendations. Your choice demonstrates the power of data-driven farming -- the soil card told you what your land needs, and you listened. Science and soil work together.

choices.label: Plant Wheat -- Staple Crop with Reliable Demand
choices.feedback: Wheat is India's second most important cereal after rice. However, your Nashik region is not traditional wheat country -- Punjab and Haryana are India's wheat bowl. Wheat also requires more water and nitrogen fertilizer, which your soil lacks. India's Green Revolution (1960s-70s), led by Dr. M.S. Swaminathan with high-yielding wheat varieties from Norman Borlaug, transformed India from a food-deficit nation to self-sufficient. But the Green Revolution's intensive wheat-rice monoculture has depleted Punjab's soil and groundwater. Sometimes the popular crop is not the right crop for your specific conditions.

choices.label: Grow Winter Vegetables -- Tomatoes, Cauliflower, Spinach
choices.feedback: Winter vegetables command premium prices but require intensive management: daily irrigation, pest monitoring, and rapid marketing (vegetables perish quickly). India is the world's second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables but loses 30-40% to post-harvest waste due to poor cold chain infrastructure. The Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana aims to build food processing and cold storage. High-value horticulture can earn 3-5x more per acre than staple crops, but the risk and labour are proportionally higher. Nashik's climate is excellent for winter vegetables.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant farm landscape in November with golden wheat fields and lush chickpea plants, sunlight casting warm hues, a nearby irrigation system, and a farmer contemplating crop choices
rounds.coaching_moment: The Rabi season is a reset opportunity — a chance to correct course after the Kharif result. Chickpea (chana) does something no other Rabi crop does: it fixes atmospheric nitrogen back into the soil, reducing your fertilizer bill next Kharif by 15-20 kg per acre. Wheat offers stability but requires irrigation at critical stages; winter vegetables offer the highest per-acre return but demand market access and post-harvest cold storage that most small farmers lack.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How might the people affected by this choice experience the outcome?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Organic Farming Debate
rounds.story: A group of farmers in your village, inspired by Subhash Palekar's Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF) movement, wants you to join them in converting to organic farming. They argue that chemical farming is destroying the soil, poisoning water, and making farmers dependent on expensive inputs. Your grandfather farmed organically by default -- there were no chemicals then. But the transition period (2-3 years) can reduce yields by 20-30% before organic premiums kick in. The government's Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) offers subsidies for organic clusters. The premium organic market in cities like Mumbai and Pune is growing rapidly.
rounds.goal: Decide whether to transition to organic farming, weighing short-term costs against long-term sustainability and health benefits.

choices.label: Convert Fully to Organic Farming
choices.feedback: You join the PKVY cluster and begin the organic transition. The first season is hard -- yields drop 25% without chemical fertilizers. But your soil health starts improving immediately. Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016. Subhash Palekar's ZBNF uses jeevamrutha (fermented cow dung culture) and mulching to build soil biology. India's organic food market is growing at 25% annually, reaching Rs 12,000 crore. The transition is painful but your grandfather smiles -- this is how he always farmed. The soil, water, and your family's health will thank you in three years.

choices.label: Try Organic on 2 Acres, Keep 3 Acres Conventional
choices.feedback: You hedge your bets -- organic on 2 acres, conventional on 3. This is actually the most common transition strategy. You can compare yields, costs, and soil health side by side. India's agricultural research system (ICAR) has documented that organic farming improves soil health, reduces input costs, and produces nutritionally superior food, but needs time to match conventional yields. Your practical approach lets you learn organic techniques while maintaining income security. Many successful Indian organic farmers started exactly this way -- test, learn, expand.

choices.label: Adopt 'Natural Farming' with Cow-Based Inputs
choices.feedback: You follow Subhash Palekar's Zero Budget Natural Farming: use your cow's dung and urine to make jeevamrutha and bijamrutha (seed treatment), apply mulch to conserve moisture, and intercrop to manage pests. ZBNF has been adopted by Andhra Pradesh as state policy, targeting 60 lakh farmers. The 'zero budget' claim means input costs drop to nearly zero since you produce your own fertilizers. India has 300 million cattle -- their dung and urine, traditionally considered sacred and useful, are the backbone of natural farming. Your input costs drop by 80% in the first season itself.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant village farm under a bright blue sky, with lush green fields and colorful crops, farmers passionately discussing organic practices near a wooden barn, sunlight illuminating their faces
rounds.coaching_moment: The organic conversion period — typically 2-3 years in India's NPOP standards — is when farmers are most vulnerable: chemical inputs are withdrawn but premium organic prices haven't kicked in yet. Full conversion on all 5 acres at once concentrates all that risk in a single season. Subhash Palekar's natural farming, based on desi cow inputs, has shown impressive results in Andhra Pradesh's zero-budget trials but requires consistent cattle access and knowledge transfer from experienced practitioners.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back, do you think this was the best use of your resources?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Monsoon Failure -- Climate Crisis
rounds.story: The following year's monsoon fails dramatically. By August, rainfall is 40% below normal. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) declares a drought in your region. Your Kharif crops are wilting, the open well is running dry, and the borewell water table has dropped 30 feet. Neighbouring farmers are selling cattle at distress prices. The Collector declares the region drought-affected, activating MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) for emergency water conservation works. You face hard choices about your farm, your livestock, and your family's immediate survival.
rounds.goal: Survive a drought crisis by making difficult decisions about resources, livestock, and accessing government relief schemes.

choices.label: Abandon the Crop and Focus on Water Conservation
choices.feedback: You stop irrigating the doomed crop and use MGNREGA funds to build farm ponds, contour bunds, and recharge structures. Maharashtra's Jalyukt Shivar Abhiyan water conservation programme has built over 6 lakh water structures across the state. Water conservation during drought is counterintuitive but visionary -- the water you save and store will determine your recovery when rain returns. India's traditional water harvesting systems (johads in Rajasthan, eri in Tamil Nadu, kere in Karnataka) were perfected over centuries. Rajendra Singh, the 'Waterman of India,' revived entire rivers through community water harvesting.

choices.label: File Crop Insurance Claim Under PMFBY
choices.feedback: You file a claim under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) -- India's crop insurance scheme that covers natural calamities including drought. The premium is heavily subsidized (just 2% for Kharif crops). Since its launch in 2016, PMFBY has covered over 5.5 crore farmer applications annually. The claim process has been improved with satellite-based crop assessment and smartphone-based damage reporting. Your insurance payout keeps your family fed during the drought. Crop insurance is not just financial protection -- it is a safety net that prevents farmer suicides during crises.

choices.label: Switch to Drought-Resistant Millets + Poultry for Income
choices.feedback: You replant with drought-resistant bajra (pearl millet) and jowar (sorghum) -- crops that evolved in semi-arid Indian conditions and need just 300mm rainfall compared to rice's 1,200mm. You also start a small poultry unit for daily income (eggs and meat). Millets are called 'climate-smart crops' because they thrive in drought and heat. India is the world's largest millet producer, and millets were staples before the Green Revolution shifted focus to wheat and rice. The National Millet Mission is reviving these nutritious, climate-resilient crops. Your grandfather farmed millets -- what was old is new again.

rounds.image_prompt: a parched agricultural landscape under a harsh sun, wilting crops in cracked soil, a dry well nearby, distressed farmers selling livestock, with a sense of urgency and despair in the air
rounds.coaching_moment: Maharashtra saw three consecutive drought years from 2014-16, triggering one of India's most severe agrarian crises. PMFBY crop insurance, when it pays out, covers yield loss against a notified threshold — but many farmers miss the notification window or don't receive the payout for 18+ months. The most resilient Nashik farmers in drought years pivoted early to millets and livestock, cutting losses by accepting a lower ceiling in exchange for a higher floor.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Is this decision optimizing for short-term or long-term outcomes? Which matters more here?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 8: The Future of Your Farm
rounds.story: After two years of farming, you sit under the neem tree where your grandfather once planned his seasons. Your farm has survived monsoon gambles, pest attacks, market volatility, and drought. You have learned that farming in India is not just about growing crops -- it is about managing risk, understanding nature, and making decisions with incomplete information. Now you must plan the long-term future: invest in technology and scale up, build a sustainable farm that preserves the land for the next generation, or explore new models like agri-tourism or farm-to-table that add value beyond raw produce. The future of Indian agriculture depends on what young farmers like you choose.
rounds.goal: Choose a long-term vision for your farm that balances profitability, sustainability, and India's food security needs.

choices.label: Invest in Precision Agriculture and Technology
choices.feedback: You install soil moisture sensors, use satellite weather data, adopt GPS-guided operations, and connect with FPOs (Farmer Producer Organizations) through digital platforms. India's AgriTech sector is booming -- startups like DeHaat, Ninjacart, and CropIn are digitizing agriculture for millions of farmers. ISRO's satellites provide crop monitoring data, and AI-powered advisory services guide planting decisions. Precision agriculture can reduce water use by 30%, fertilizer use by 20%, and increase yields by 15%. You become a Digital Kisaan -- combining your grandfather's wisdom with 21st-century technology.

choices.label: Build a Model Sustainable Farm (Organic + Water Harvesting)
choices.feedback: You create a showcase of sustainable farming: organic crops, farm ponds for water harvesting, solar-powered micro-irrigation, vermicompost pits, and integrated farming (crops + fish + poultry + trees). Your farm becomes a 'Food Forest' inspired by Subhash Palekar and Masanobu Fukuoka's natural farming philosophies. NABARD's Watershed Development programme and National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) provide funding support. Your farm becomes a training centre -- other farmers visit to learn. Sustainable agriculture is not going backwards; it is the most sophisticated form of farming, combining ecology, economics, and traditional knowledge into a system that can feed India forever.

choices.label: Join/Start a Farmer Producer Organization (FPO)
choices.feedback: You join 50 neighbouring farmers to form an FPO -- a collective that pools resources, negotiates better prices, and accesses credit and technology as a group. India's goal of establishing 10,000 FPOs by 2027 (with Rs 6,865 crore budget) recognizes that small and marginal farmers (86% of Indian farmers hold less than 2 hectares) need collective strength. Amul's cooperative model transformed Indian dairy; FPOs aim to do the same for agriculture. Together, your FPO negotiates directly with exporters, bypasses middlemen, and secures bulk discounts on inputs. Collective action is the most powerful tool for India's small farmers.

choices.label: Diversify into Agri-Tourism and Farm-to-Table
choices.feedback: You add farm-stay rooms, organize farm experience tours for city families, and start a farm-to-table venture supplying organic produce directly to Nashik and Pune restaurants. Maharashtra is India's agri-tourism pioneer -- the state's agri-tourism policy has created over 3,000 farm tourism centres. Urban families pay Rs 2,000-5,000 per day to experience farming life. Your revenue diversifies beyond crop income. This model works particularly well near cities and tourist destinations. Nashik, with its vineyards and proximity to Mumbai, is perfect. Your farm becomes a bridge between India's rural heritage and urban curiosity.

rounds.image_prompt: a serene Indian farm under a sprawling neem tree, lush green fields stretching out, tools and seedlings scattered nearby, warm sunlight filtering through leaves, a sense of hope and reflection
rounds.coaching_moment: Precision agriculture — soil sensors, drone-based nutrient mapping, variable rate fertilizer application — is no longer science fiction in Maharashtra. Pilot programs in Pune district showed 18% reduction in input costs and 12% yield increase on the same land. But technology without community adoption creates fragmented advantages; Farmer Producer Organizations let smallholders pool resources, negotiate collectively with buyers, and share the cost of technology that no single 5-acre farm could justify alone.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If this were a real business decision, what extra information would you want?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

glossary_terms.definition: India's three agricultural seasons. Kharif (June-October) is the monsoon season for rice, cotton, soybean, and maize. Rabi (November-April) is the winter season for wheat, chickpea, and mustard. Zaid (April-June) is the short summer season for watermelon, cucumber, and moong dal. Crop planning across these seasons is fundamental to Indian farming.

A price set by the Government of India at which it purchases crops from farmers, ensuring they receive a minimum return regardless of market conditions. The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) recommends MSP for 23 crops. MSP is a critical safety net but implementation and coverage remain debated.

India's crop insurance scheme launched in 2016, replacing earlier schemes. Farmers pay a small premium (2% for Kharif, 1.5% for Rabi) and the government subsidizes the rest. It covers yield losses from natural calamities, pests, and diseases. Satellite-based assessment and smartphone reporting have improved the claims process.

A government scheme launched in 2015 that provides farmers with a card containing information about the nutrient status of their soil along with recommendations for appropriate dosage of nutrients. Over 23 crore soil health cards have been distributed, promoting scientific and balanced use of fertilizers.

A farming method promoted by Subhash Palekar that uses cow dung-based natural inputs (jeevamrutha, bijamrutha), mulching, and intercropping to eliminate external chemical inputs. 'Zero budget' refers to near-zero cost of inputs. Andhra Pradesh has adopted ZBNF as state policy, targeting 60 lakh farmers. It is rooted in traditional Indian agricultural practices.

cultural_context: Scientific literacy is a strategic priority under NEP 2020, which emphasises inquiry-based learning over rote memorisation. Krishi Katha: The Farming Seasons builds the analytical instincts that support strong performance in India's science curricula.
coaching_moment: Every choice shapes your strategy — great leaders think several steps ahead before deciding.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
